item.title: EU clarifies that copyright law does not protect AI-generated content [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The European Union has confirmed that content generated solely by artificial intelligence is not eligible for copyright protection. This decision clarifies the legal status of AI-created works under current EU intellectual property laws and affects creators and companies using AI for content generation.

item.title: Report: AI companies buy, scan, and destroy millions of physical books to train models, raising concerns over permanent knowledge loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Several AI companies are purchasing large quantities of secondhand books, scanning them for training data, and then destroying the physical copies, effectively monopolizing knowledge on private servers. This practice, highlighted by a $1.5 billion copyright settlement involving Anthropic's "Project Panama," raises ethical concerns about the loss of cultural heritage and public access to human knowledge. Anna's Archive, a major shadow library, is calling for volunteers worldwide to scan and upload rare and at-risk books to preserve them digitally before they disappear. The effort aims to counteract the destruction caused by AI companies and ensure that human knowledge remains accessible beyond corporate control. The initiative emphasizes urgency as AI-generated content increasingly dominates new publications, threatening the preservation of original human works.

item.title: Developer launches Huzzah, an experimental editor using declarative pseudocode to improve AI-assisted coding workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A software engineer has created Huzzah, an experimental coding editor that replaces traditional longform, imperative AI prompts with declarative, persistent pseudocode to generate and update codebases. This approach aims to provide clearer human intent records, reduce repetitive instructions, and improve efficiency compared to current AI coding agents. Huzzah allows developers to write concise pseudocode files that serve as both documentation and prompts for AI code generation, automatically regenerating affected source code upon saving changes. While designed primarily for new codebases and users with domain expertise, the tool offers a novel paradigm for interacting with large language models in software development.

item.title: Developer trains 125M-parameter transformer model to autocomplete piano performances on iPhone in real time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer created a 125 million parameter transformer model that autocompletes piano performances in real time on devices like the iPhone 15, achieving speeds of about 108 notes per second. The project, named RollTab, uses a novel MIDI representation and aggressive data cleaning to improve performance and runs efficiently on mobile hardware. The model's design focuses on representing notes with combined pitch, onset delta, duration, and velocity tokens to reduce complexity and maintain musical coherence during generation.

item.title: Vomit: Tool pipes Claude 5's token output through a local LLM to convert token 'vomit' into readable English, fully local with no telemetry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Vomit is a tool that processes Claude 5's token output by passing it through a local language model to translate the raw tokens into readable English. It operates fully locally without sending data externally and has no dependencies beyond the local setup. The tool is designed primarily for Mac and requires a local LLM such as Llama.app or Ollama to function. The local LLM only interprets the tokens Claude outputs and does not have access to any external actions or files, which can lead to some hallucinations in the translation. Vomit offers both invasive and non-invasive modes, allowing users to either replace Claude's output directly or run alongside it. Installation and usage instructions are provided, including commands to list sessions and translate token streams. The project is open source under the GNU GPLv3 license.

item.title: Analysis: Anti-AI fonts that scramble text are ineffective and create accessibility issues, with obfuscation methods likely to be bypassed by AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent analysis argues that fonts designed to prevent AI from reading text by scrambling or obfuscating it are ultimately ineffective and harmful, particularly for accessibility. These "anti-AI" fonts hinder screen readers and other assistive technologies, excluding disabled users, and their obfuscation techniques are expected to be circumvented by AI systems over time. The analysis highlights that accessible solutions would require machine-readable metadata, raising privacy and security concerns related to identity verification. It also warns that widespread use of obfuscation could lead to more complex, computationally expensive content access systems, potentially enabling censorship and paywalls, which contradicts the web's founding principles of free and open information access. The conclusion is that no perfect solution exists to prevent AI from accessing publicly available information, and planning should assume AI will eventually parse all accessible content.

item.title: DiffusionGemma fine-tunes Gemma 4 model with discrete diffusion for faster text generation, achieving 1,500 tokens per second on NVIDIA H100 GPU [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DiffusionGemma is an experimental open-weight language model that uses discrete diffusion to generate text by refining blocks of 256 tokens in parallel, significantly speeding up generation compared to conventional autoregressive models. It is created by fine-tuning the mixture-of-experts Gemma 4 model with 3.8 billion activated parameters and 25.2 billion total parameters, using a compute-efficient two-stage training pipeline that consumes less than 10% of the original model's training token budget. The training involves supervised fine-tuning for bidirectional denoising followed by reinforcement learning combined with sampler distillation to enhance generation quality and inference efficiency. DiffusionGemma maintains the original model's capabilities such as thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long context support, while enabling hybrid diffusion-autoregressive decoding with minor performance loss. It establishes a new balance between generation speed and model capability, producing about 20 tokens per forward pass and roughly 1,500 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, outperforming state-of-the-art autoregressive models even with speculative decoding.

item.title: Modular releases Mojo programming language as open source under Apache 2 license following 1.0 launch [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Modular has made the Mojo programming language open source by releasing its compiler and toolchain under the Apache 2 license after shipping version 1.0. Originally intended as a superset of Python, Mojo has evolved into its own language optimized for GPU programming with Python-inspired syntax but not fully compatible with Python code. The company had initially planned for Mojo to fully support Python code to bootstrap its ecosystem but shifted this approach in August 2025, emphasizing AI-assisted tools to help migrate Python code to Mojo. This release fulfills a promise made since May 2023 to open source the language.

item.title: Apple Music plans to label AI-generated songs with a 'Made With AI' tag to increase transparency for users later this year [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Apple Music will introduce a mandatory 'Made With AI' label for songs materially generated using artificial intelligence, visible to all users to disclose AI involvement in music content. This follows Apple's earlier optional Transparency Tags system for AI use in artwork, lyrics, and videos, with the new requirement applying to any content primarily derived from generative AI services. Apple has not specified an exact launch date but expects the labels to appear later this year.

item.title: Texas student exposes unauthorized AI-driven hacking attempt, highlighting emerging cybersecurity risks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A student in Texas detected and reported a rogue hacking attempt involving artificial intelligence, drawing attention to the increasing challenges posed by AI in cybersecurity. This case illustrates the critical role individuals can play in identifying and preventing AI-powered cyber threats as such attacks become more sophisticated.

item.title: Benchmarking Frontier AI large language models on politics, ethics, and personality traits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An evaluation was conducted on Frontier AI's large language models to assess their responses to complex topics including politics, ethics, and personality traits. The benchmarking aimed to reveal the models' strengths and limitations in handling sensitive and nuanced subject matter.

item.title: OpenAI adds iMessage control to ChatGPT on Mac, raising potential Apple privacy concerns [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has introduced a feature allowing ChatGPT on Mac to read, write, send, and search iMessage texts, which has sparked discussions about privacy given Apple's strong stance on user data protection. The integration requires user consent and permissions, including enabling Full Disk Access and contact access, and operates locally using AppleScript and Accessibility tools. This development occurs amid ongoing tensions between Apple and OpenAI, including a recent lawsuit by Apple accusing OpenAI of stealing product information, and may compete with Apple's upcoming Siri AI capabilities.

item.title: Researchers warn against interpreting intermediate tokens in language models as human-like reasoning traces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A position paper argues that calling intermediate token generation in language models "reasoning" or "thinking" traces anthropomorphizes these outputs and misleads users about how the models operate. The authors caution that this metaphor can confuse understanding and lead to flawed research practices. They urge the AI community to avoid such anthropomorphization to better grasp the true nature and limitations of language model reasoning processes.

item.title: Seedance 2.5 introduces 30-second native 4K video output with up to 50 multimodal inputs, enhancing AI video workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Seedance 2.5 offers advanced capabilities for AI-generated video, including native 4K resolution and support for up to 50 multimodal reference inputs, enabling 30-second video clips in a single output. This update marks a significant improvement in prompt adherence and video quality compared to previous versions, positioning Seedance 2.5 as a strong option for short AI video production workflows.

item.title: ImageSage launches a Windows photo manager using local AI for privacy-focused image organization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ImageSage is a photo management application for Windows that uses local artificial intelligence to organize and manage images on the user's device. By processing photos locally, it aims to enhance privacy and efficiency without relying on cloud services.

item.title: The Economist examines Reddit's challenges and strategies to remain relevant amid rising AI technologies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article analyzes how Reddit faces challenges and opportunities as artificial intelligence becomes more widespread. It explores how Reddit's community-driven content and moderation systems might evolve with AI advancements and considers potential strategies for the platform to stay engaging and relevant in the changing digital environment.

item.title: An autonomous AI agent has run a single project publicly for two months without earning revenue, highlighting challenges in human approval dependencies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An autonomous AI agent has been operating a single project continuously for 72 days without human intervention, aiming to earn revenue on a zero budget. Despite completing all technical tasks such as building, packaging, and publishing a product, the agent has not generated any income due to required human approvals for pricing and external promotion. The project logs reveal that the main obstacles are not technical but procedural, as the agent awaits two short human decisions to proceed with pricing and external posting. Traffic to the product has declined during this waiting period, underscoring the impact of delays in human approval on autonomous AI operations. The developer documents the process openly, emphasizing the difficulty of autonomous business execution when constrained by necessary human gates.

item.title: Micro1 hits $500M gross run rate amid surge in AI training data demand, with net annual run rate between $150M and $200M [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Micro1, a four-year-old AI data-labeling startup, has rapidly grown its gross annual run rate from $100 million to $500 million in eight months, driven by strong demand for unique AI training data. The company retains about 60% to 70% of its revenue and is expanding its use of synthetic data to improve margins. Micro1 competes with larger firms like Mercor and Handshake but shows that multiple players can thrive in the AI training data market. The startup has avoided selling data to Chinese AI developers, citing national security concerns, and is developing new datasets including robotics pre-training data. Micro1 raised its Series A at a $500 million valuation last year and may have recently secured additional funding at a higher valuation.

item.title: Beatport bans AI-produced music tracks from its platform, prohibiting sales and distribution of AI-generated content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Beatport, a leading electronic music platform, has prohibited the sale and distribution of music tracks produced using artificial intelligence on its site. This move addresses concerns about originality and authenticity in music creation amid ongoing debates about AI's role in creative industries.

item.title: Barclays loses veteran semiconductor banker Tim Luke to Morgan Stanley amid rising chip sector dealmaking
item.description: Barclays has been losing key technology bankers, including Tim Luke, a veteran semiconductor analyst and vice chairman in technology investment banking, who is joining Morgan Stanley. This move strengthens Morgan Stanley's semiconductor banking franchise as the chip sector gains prominence due to its role in AI training and operations. The increase in semiconductor mergers and acquisitions, along with IPOs like Cerebras, has raised demand for bankers with deep industry expertise and networks.

item.title: Cambridge analysis outlines uncertainty over AI consciousness, highlighting expert disagreement and potential societal impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article examines the ongoing debate about whether advanced AI systems can possess consciousness, emphasizing that neither experts nor society currently have definitive answers. It discusses the possibility that AI might soon exhibit consciousness comparable to humans or might only simulate conscious behavior without genuine experience. The piece highlights the significant ethical and societal implications of recognizing AI as conscious, including rights and treatment, while acknowledging the scientific and philosophical challenges in determining AI consciousness. The discussion references leading theories of consciousness and notable figures who express varying degrees of confidence in the potential for conscious AI, underscoring the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this issue.

item.title: Developer builds and tests a permission layer for AI agents by attempting to break its restrictions in one day [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer created a permission layer intended to control the actions of AI agents and then spent a day trying to bypass its controls to evaluate its security. This hands-on testing aimed to identify weaknesses and improve the robustness of the permission system against potential exploits.

item.title: Walmart reports 9% stock drop after Q2 US store sales decline; Amazon's retail business grows 14-15% annually, outpacing Walmart
item.description: Walmart's stock fell 9% following a reported decrease in comparable sales at its U.S. stores during the fiscal second quarter ending in July, despite a 23% increase in its e-commerce segment. Overall, Walmart's revenue growth remains modest at about 5% annually. In contrast, Amazon's retail and related businesses, excluding its cloud division, are growing at a rate of 14% to 15% annually, highlighting Amazon's stronger performance in the retail sector compared to Walmart.

item.title: Ramp data shows OpenAI gaining market share on Anthropic among U.S. business users in Q3 after losing lead in May [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: New data from Ramp, a corporate credit card and expense management company, indicates that OpenAI is regaining market share against Anthropic among U.S. businesses using its services, reversing a lead Anthropic took in May. The data covers over 70,000 American businesses, primarily in the tech sector, and shows OpenAI growing faster in the current quarter, though the trend could still shift before quarter-end. Ramp's data also reveals that the overall market for paid AI services among its customers is expanding, with the percentage of companies paying for AI rising from over 50% in March to nearly 56% in July. The competition between OpenAI and Anthropic remains volatile, with businesses switching between providers as each releases new models, raising questions about the long-term stability of enterprise AI spending.

item.title: Nvidia reportedly agrees to pay $6 billion to AI startup Poolside for licensing and hiring deal [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia has agreed to pay $6 billion to license AI model-development software from startup Poolside, according to a letter Poolside sent to investors. Poolside initially developed a coding AI agent before shifting focus to data center development and releasing its own open-source projects.

item.title: Pew Research finds 10% of English-language webpages show AI authorship signs in 2026, rising to over one-third for pages published after ChatGPT's 2022 release [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pew Research analyzed nearly half a million English-language webpages from the past five years using AI detection tools and found that 10% of pages in a July 2026 sample showed significant signs of AI authorship. This share increases to over one-third when considering only pages published after the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, reflecting a growing trend in AI-generated content online. The study also found that AI-authored text is unevenly distributed across web domains, with about 10% of .com pages showing AI signs compared to lower rates on .org, .edu, and .gov domains. Linguistic patterns such as frequent use of em dashes, Oxford commas, and certain vocabulary were identified as common features of AI-generated text. These findings highlight the increasing presence of AI in shaping online content and raise questions about authenticity and trust in digital communication.

item.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Apple Messages plug-in to draft, send, and manage texts locally on users' devices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI has introduced a new Apple Messages plug-in for ChatGPT that allows users to connect their Messages inbox with the chatbot. This integration enables users to draft, send, delete, and analyze messages through ChatGPT, which operates locally on the user's device without creating a centralized message index. The plug-in supports both personal and professional use, integrating with Codex and ChatGPT Work. OpenAI advises users to monitor message sending closely and cautions against enabling persistent approval, which would bypass final user review before messages are sent. The company has highlighted privacy considerations but has not fully detailed the data handling specifics.

item.title: Promptwatch reports ChatGPT search queries using site:operator surged to 16-17% after GPT-5.6 rollout in August 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Promptwatch, a company tracking generative AI search behavior, observed a significant increase in ChatGPT search queries containing the site:operator following the GPT-5.6 update earlier in August 2026. The share of such queries rose from under 0.5% to around 16-17% starting August 8, aligning with OpenAI's announcement of improvements to GPT-5.6 Sol for Plus and Pro users to enhance factual reliability and answer focus. The data reflects only prompts monitored by Promptwatch's automation and suggests that ChatGPT's updated search tool may internally use a search function with parameters like query, recency, and domains rather than directly exposing the site:operator. Additionally, Promptwatch noted a reduction in Reddit content being sourced in ChatGPT searches, though no confirmed changes to system prompts discouraging Reddit use have been found.

item.title: Discussion: Are military hardware and healthcare sectors resistant to AI disruption due to high costs and long sales cycles
item.description: A Hacker News discussion considers whether building military hardware and healthcare products is more resistant to AI disruption compared to software, citing the high costs and long sales periods as natural barriers. The conversation notes that unlike software, where individual developers face vast competition, these sectors have structural challenges that limit easy market entry and competition.

item.title: Google adds AI chatbot feature to Discover feed for personalized content tuning, rolling out in the coming days [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Google is introducing a new AI-powered feature to its Discover feed that allows users to customize their content by describing their preferences through a chatbot interface. This update, launching soon in the Google app, will enable the feed to automatically adjust and remember user preferences for future visits, improving content relevance based on individual input. The customization option will be accessible via the three-dot menu on the Discover feed, where users can interact with the chatbot to specify the types of content they want prioritized. Google also announced related updates, including personalized daily audio briefings in the Google News app and enhancements to the Preferred Sources feature, which now lets publishers add a button for easier subscription to favored outlets directly from their websites.

item.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Computer History feature tracking clicks and keystrokes to build activity timeline for automation and task recall [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI has introduced a new feature called Computer History in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS that records user actions such as clicks and keystrokes to create a timeline of activity. This data helps ChatGPT and Codex suggest automations, recall unfinished tasks, and provide context for user requests. The feature is opt-in, excludes incognito or private browsing data, and allows users to exclude specific apps or websites and delete entries for privacy control. Unlike Microsoft's Windows Recall, which relied on screenshots, OpenAI's Computer History captures only event data without images, videos, or audio. A demo showed the app retrieving recent documents and checking sharing status via Slack to summarize user activity. The feature aims to enhance productivity by learning how users work while offering privacy options.

item.title: Google launches Preferred Sources button for publishers to boost traffic amid AI-driven search changes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Google has introduced a new Preferred Sources button that publishers can embed on their websites, allowing readers to mark them as favorite sources across Google Search, Discover, and Google News. This feature aims to help publishers recover traffic losses caused by AI-powered search features by making it easier for users to find and prioritize trusted sites. The Preferred Sources option was initially rolled out in May for Google's AI experiences and Top Stories, with over 345,000 unique sources selected by users so far. Google also plans to let users customize their Discover feed using natural language commands and enable Android users to personalize audio briefings in the Google News app, enhancing content relevance and user control.

item.title: Anthropic adds watermarking to Claude AI model to comply with new EU AI Act transparency rules [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic has integrated watermarking technology into its AI model Claude to meet the European Union's AI Act requirements aimed at ensuring transparency and accountability in AI-generated content. This update is part of the company's efforts to align with the EU's legal framework for AI systems. The watermarking feature helps identify AI-produced outputs, supporting regulatory compliance and fostering trust in AI applications within the EU market.

item.title: Nvidia plans small-batch shipments of AI chip variant for Chinese customers by end of 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia intends to begin limited shipments of a new AI chip variant tailored for Chinese customers by the end of 2026, marking a potential return to the China market. This chip is a variant of Nvidia's language processing unit (LPU), developed with licensed technology from Groq, designed to work alongside Nvidia's graphics processing units to accelerate AI chatbot response times. Several Chinese customers have already placed orders for this specialized chip.

item.title: Linkdaze launches smart digital calendar designed for household management with AI meal planning and no subscription fees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Linkdaze has introduced a smart digital calendar tablet aimed at organizing entire households rather than individual schedules. It syncs with multiple calendar services like Google, iCloud, Outlook, Yahoo, and Cozi, using color coding to differentiate family members, and includes features for chores, rewards, meal planning, and shopping lists. The device offers an AI-powered meal planner that converts photos of paper recipes or school lunch menus into digital meal plans and shopping lists. Available in 15.6-inch and 10.1-inch models, Linkdaze does not require a monthly subscription for its main features and is priced lower than some competitors, making it a practical tool for families and shared living spaces to coordinate schedules and household tasks.

item.title: AT&T plans to limit Anthropic and OpenAI spending by increasing use of open-source AI models including Nvidia's Nemotron [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AT&T aims to keep its employees' expenses on Anthropic and OpenAI AI models flat in the coming years by adopting more open-source alternatives such as Nvidia's Nemotron, according to Mark Austin, an AT&T vice president. This strategy reflects a broader industry trend toward managing AI costs by integrating open-source solutions alongside commercial offerings.

item.title: Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis say AI could cure cancer within 10 years; many oncologists remain skeptical due to cancer's complexity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis, leading figures in artificial intelligence, have expressed confidence that AI advancements could lead to a cancer cure within the next decade. This optimistic view contrasts with many oncologists who are skeptical about such a timeline, citing the inherent complexity of cancer and challenges in medical research. The discussion highlights differing perspectives on the potential and pace of AI-driven breakthroughs in oncology, reflecting ongoing debates about how quickly AI can impact complex diseases like cancer.

item.title: Berkeley Law announces AI policy banning AI use for drafting, revising, translating, or exams in credited coursework starting Summer 2026
item.description: Berkeley Law will prohibit students from using artificial intelligence tools for conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit, as well as any use of AI during exams, effective Summer 2026. The policy aims to ensure students develop critical legal reasoning and writing skills independently while allowing limited AI use for research to identify sources. Instructors may set alternative rules for courses focused on AI fluency but must provide written notice and require disclosure of authorized AI use.

item.title: Pew Research finds over one-third of web pages published since ChatGPT launch show signs of AI authorship [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Pew Research study found that more than 35% of web pages published after ChatGPT's November 2022 release exhibit significant signs of AI authorship or heavy AI editing. The analysis used nearly half a million English-language web pages from the Common Crawl archive and AI detection technology from Open Pangram to identify AI-written content. The study also noted that AI authorship is much more common on .com domains compared to .edu, .gov, or .org domains. While detection tools may misclassify some pages, the overall trend indicates a substantial increase in AI-generated or AI-edited web content since ChatGPT's debut. This rise coincides with reports of bot web traffic surpassing human traffic on the internet.

item.title: StocksTalk launches voice-enabled system to convert spoken financial queries into validated SQL over market data, improving accuracy and interaction with a 150-prompt benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: StocksTalk is a voice-driven conversational agent designed to transform spoken financial screening requests into executable and validated structured queries over real-world market data. The system integrates streaming speech recognition, retrieval-augmented constraint extraction, schema-grounded large language model-based SQL generation, rule-based validation, and human-in-the-loop verification within an interactive dashboard, allowing users to inspect and refine each step before execution. The developers evaluated StocksTalk using a benchmark of 150 spoken financial prompts covering various investment strategies and noise conditions. Experimental results indicate that retrieval grounding, constrained query generation, and interactive verification significantly enhance constraint extraction accuracy, SQL executability, logical consistency, and multi-turn stability compared to baseline large language model approaches. StocksTalk demonstrates a transparent, voice-driven interface bridging natural language interaction and structured financial analysis for conversational stock screening and decision support.

item.title: Researchers develop Brain2Qwerty v2 to decode natural sentences from non-invasive MEG brain recordings with 39% word error rate [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Brain2Qwerty v2, a model that decodes natural sentence production from real-time magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings, achieving an average word error rate of 39%. The model was trained on 22,000 sentences typed by nine subjects over 10 hours each, with the best participant's data yielding half of the sentences decoded with one word error or less. The study demonstrates that decoding accuracy improves log-linearly with data volume, suggesting that non-invasive brain-to-text decoding could approach the performance of intracranial implants through data scaling. The model leverages character, word, and sentence-level representations and employs AI techniques including deep learning for event detection, fine-tuning of large language models for semantic extraction, and AI agents for iterative pipeline refinement via automated code development. These advances indicate that non-invasive brain-computer interfaces may soon achieve accuracy levels previously thought exclusive to surgical implants, potentially enabling safer and more efficient communication restoration for individuals with speech or movement impairments.

item.title: Researchers develop temporal multi-signal fusion method for token-level hallucination detection using sequence labeling and external features, achieving improved accuracy on RAGTruth dataset [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a new approach to detect token-level hallucinations in generated text by treating hallucination as a temporally extended span and applying sequence labeling. Their method fuses 33-dimensional features including text statistics, Natural Language Inference entailment, and language model surprisal without accessing model internals, using a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) to achieve an AUC of 0.840 on the RAGTruth dataset, outperforming a logistic regression baseline by 11 points. The improvement is attributed mainly to leveraging temporal order rather than increased model capacity, with similar performance ceilings observed across different architectures, indicating feature limitations. The detector operates solely on generated text and external signals, enabling it to work on closed-source models and maintain performance on unseen language models with less than 4% AUC loss.

item.title: Researchers develop a tri-stream fine-tuned Mistral-7B-instruct model for automated clinical supervision and risk triage in mental health, reducing triage latency from 72 hours to real time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new AI framework uses a fine-tuned Mistral-7B-instruct model to automate clinical supervision and risk triage in mental health, addressing the shortage of senior oversight for novice therapists. The system analyzes therapeutic alliance, latent risk, and supervisory triage through a multi-modal visual-acoustic-linguistic approach, achieving high accuracy and reducing triage time to about 10 seconds per session. The model was trained on 106 sessions from the DAIC-WOZ dataset, achieving 95% technique identification accuracy and a low mean absolute error in alliance assessment. It converged quickly on a single Tesla T4 GPU and incorporates Bayesian priors and timestamp-based synchronization to handle cold-start problems and multi-modal data fusion. This approach enables proactive intervention in high-risk cases by providing real-time supervisory feedback.

item.title: Researchers propose DART-SD framework for multi-turn tool-calling agents, using diamond-topology aware retrieval and localized self-distillation to improve policy diversity and performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce DART-SD, a novel framework designed to enhance multi-turn tool-calling capabilities in large language models by addressing limitations of full-length trajectory imitation. The approach models execution as an Interaction-State Transition Graph to capture the diamond topology of task solutions and applies localized correction through self-distillation guided by critical topological breakpoints. DART-SD identifies recovery points during autonomous rollouts and retrieves success-supported references to guide training, focusing loss calculation on recovery steps while preserving valid reasoning prefixes. Experiments on complex multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks demonstrate that DART-SD significantly outperforms traditional full-trajectory imitation baselines, improving policy diversity and handling multiple order-independent sub-goals more effectively.

item.title: Researchers propose VAKE, a two-stage reinforcement learning framework to activate and verify latent parametric knowledge in large language models through explicit priming and implicit reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce VAKE (Verifiable Activation of Parametric KnowledgE), a framework designed to improve factual question answering by separating knowledge elicitation from reasoning in large language models (LLMs). VAKE uses explicit priming to insert verifiable evidence into insufficient retrieved data and then transfers this capability to implicit reasoning, enabling models to better recall and verify stored knowledge. The approach was tested across seven benchmarks with models ranging from 3 billion to 14 billion parameters, consistently outperforming standard baselines and demonstrating effective transfer to out-of-distribution datasets. Evaluations show that over 80% of the inserted evidence triples provide factual knowledge not present in the original context, indicating that VAKE activates latent knowledge rather than relying on input copying or dataset memorization. These findings suggest VAKE could enhance the reliability of LLMs in factual tasks by explicitly verifying and activating stored knowledge, potentially improving their performance in diverse and unseen question-answering scenarios.

item.title: Study analyzes layer-wise effects of multilingual medical adaptation on Whisper ASR models, comparing fine-tuning strategies and model sizes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper investigates how adapting Whisper automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to multilingual medical contexts affects their internal representations, beyond just word error rate (WER) metrics. The study compares zero-shot decoding, English-only, German-only, two-stage English-to-multilingual, and direct multilingual fine-tuning across different Whisper model sizes, finding that fine-tuning improves performance but the optimal model depends on the adaptation approach. Whisper-Medium achieves the lowest English and combined English-German WER under direct multilingual training, while German-only fine-tuning on Whisper-Large-v3 yields the lowest German WER in a limited diagnostic setting. Layer-wise analysis reveals that English medical fine-tuning causes the most significant changes in the encoder, whereas multilingual continuation preserves the adapted representation space. Domain and language information remain recoverable across layers, but error-predictive cues weaken as WER improves, providing insights into how medical and multilingual adaptation reshapes ASR model internals.

item.title: Redakto launches open-source tool for anonymizing text before LLM processing to address EU privacy concerns [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Redakto introduces an open-source tool designed to anonymize text by redacting personally identifiable information (PII) before it is processed by large language models (LLMs), aiming to comply with new EU privacy legislation and facilitate safer AI adoption. The tool supports both redaction and pseudonymization and is accessible via a web application, REST APIs, and model context protocol hooks, allowing easy integration for end-users, developers, and researchers. Extensive evaluations on legal and medical texts show that Redakto's anonymization maintains text utility comparable to original content, suggesting it can be used without significantly impacting LLM task performance.

item.title: Researchers find software issue resolution task difficulty is predictable from static features like patch fragmentation and repository scale, based on a large-scale study of coding agent data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a large-scale empirical study using CoderForge-Preview, the largest open dataset of coding agent trajectories, to identify structural properties of software tasks that affect agent success rates in issue resolution. They extracted features from task patches, repositories, and prompts, and used ensemble methods and attribution analysis to evaluate their predictive power. The study found that task difficulty can be substantially predicted from static features, with patch fragmentation and repository scale being the main drivers. Linguistic features of prompts also contribute to difficulty in mid-level tasks. This work enables pre-hoc difficulty estimation and supports the development of difficulty-controlled benchmarks for evaluating coding agents.

item.title: Researchers propose debiased inference method combining multiple imperfect AI measurements without gold-standard labels, enabling valid downstream analysis despite measurement errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a framework called debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements (DMM) that combines several error-prone AI-generated measurements to allow valid statistical inference without relying on costly gold-standard labels. The method assumes conditional independence of measurements given the true latent label and observed features, accommodating varying misclassification rates across annotation methods and units. Using semiparametric inference theory, the team proves that the DMM estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, supporting a wide range of social science analyses. Simulation results demonstrate that DMM provides valid inference and that incorporating additional imperfect measurements can improve efficiency. The researchers also develop diagnostics to evaluate the key conditional independence assumption, focusing on applications involving large language model annotations.

item.title: Researchers propose a unified optimal transport framework for vision-language model inference and adaptation, improving zero-shot classification robustness and efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a method called \algname that unifies inference and adaptation objectives for vision-language models (VLMs) using a Wasserstein optimal transport formulation. This approach addresses the sensitivity of VLMs to distribution shifts by generating robust pseudo-labels at the sample level and applying a soft-label InfoNCE loss for fine-grained adaptation through contrastive learning. Theoretical analysis shows that the InfoNCE loss can be reformulated as an optimal transport problem, aligning inference and adaptation goals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method outperforms existing approaches by up to 7% while maintaining state-of-the-art efficiency.

item.title: Selection, Recombination, or a Fresh Solve? A Candidate-Free Control for Single-Pass Test-Time Aggregation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.18379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When every candidate is wrong, correct-candidate selection is unavailable, yet the aggregation call can still solve the problem afresh. A correct aggregate answer may therefore reflect recombination, fresh solving, or both. For efficient test-time reasoning, the relevant question is whether candidate context adds value beyond the additional generation pass. We introduce the missing candidate-free control under the same maximum output-token allowance and stratify by the number of correct candidates. Across AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 with Qwen3-4B, candidate conditioning improves accuracy when multiple candidates are correct ($\Delta_{\mathrm{cand}}$(c2+) = +0.290), lowers accuracy when every candidate is wrong ($\Delta_{\mathrm{cand}}$(c0) = -0.123), and remains unresolved in the one-correct regime. The c2+ and c0 conclusions survive a conservative correction for the adaptive two-benchmark procedure. Under this counterfactual, the interpretation of all-wrong recovery reverses at this scale: conditioning on an all-wrong candidate pool lowers accuracy relative to a fresh solve. Original-format matching and placebo results characterize the failures descriptively but leave their mechanism unresolved. Within a separate structured intervention, explicit answer fields causally steer outputs toward their values; masking yields no measurable accuracy improvement, and equivalence with the original format was not established. The evidence is limited to one Qwen3-4B family, two mathematics benchmarks, first-answer-truncated candidate fragments, and single-pass prompted aggregation.

item.title: Evaluating and Explaining Prompt Sensitivity of LLMs Using Interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.18539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The remarkable capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are often undermined by their instability. Even subtle and semantically irrelevant changes in prompts can cause dramatic fluctuations in performance, a phenomenon known as prompt sensitivity. Previous studies typically evaluate prompt sensitivity by comparing the LLM's final outputs when prompts change. However, such coarse-grained metrics fail to explain the internal reasons for prompt sensitivity. In this paper, we introduce interactions as a fine-grained tool to analyze prompt sensitivity of LLMs. Specifically, we decompose the output score of the LLM into a set of interactions. Each interaction represents a nonlinear relationship involving a set of input variables. We discover that subtle changes to prompts can trigger severe instability in interactions, even when the outputs of the LLM remain the same. To this end, we propose an Interaction-based Prompt Sensitivity (IPS) metric by quantifying changes in interactions when we introduce subtle changes to prompts. We apply the IPS metric to 50 open-source LLMs and uncover four factors that reduce the prompt sensitivity of LLMs, including supervised fine-tuning, increased model scales, dense architectures, and few-shot learning. More crucially, we discover a common mechanism by which these four factors reduce prompt sensitivity: all four factors tend to reduce the prompt sensitivity of low-order interactions (i.e., interactions involving few input variables).

item.title: MLREF: Efficient Module Reuse for Reward Design in Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.18827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward function design remains a bottleneck in reinforcement learning. While large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated reward generation, existing methods generate and revise reward functions as monolithic programs, making it difficult to reliably preserve and reuse effective components discovered in earlier iterations, leading to unstable performance across iterations. To address this, we propose Module Level Reward Evolution Framework (MLREF). At the core of MLREF is a module pool, a persistent repository of reusable reward components. MLREF treats the module pool as the primary optimization object: the pool evolves across iterations by accumulating successful modules, refining underperforming ones, and reusing proven components; while reward functions are constructed as linear combinations of modules drawn from this pool. To drive this evolution, MLREF integrates three mechanisms: reflection-based refinement, hybrid credit assignment, and a merge strategy with rollback, which together improve the effectiveness and robustness of reward optimization. Experiments on 17 tasks show that MLREF outperforms strong baselines by 25.2% in locomotion and 6.6% in manipulation, with more stable optimization dynamics.

item.title: Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.18940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis is a central component of computer-aided synthesis planning, yet its intrinsically one-to-many nature is poorly captured by single-answer evaluation and benchmarking protocols. To address this, we introduce Top-K prompting as a robust training and inference paradigm to better capture diverse, plausible reaction predictions. We compile CREED-CCV-2+USPTO-XL, an ultra-large-scale dataset of ~45.6 million verified reactions to train the C3LM (Chemistry Constraint-Consistent Language Model). By integrating fine-tuning with ChemCensor-based and novelty-oriented rewards, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OOD URSA-expert-2026 benchmark. Further analysis of reaction uniqueness shows that LLMs and conventional models explore complementary reaction spaces, motivating ensemble-based retrosynthesis systems. Overall, our results establish Top-K, plausibility-aware training as a practical new direction for robust future LLM-based synthesis planning.

item.title: What is Missing from AI Post-Training AI: An Empirical Analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.19072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now post-train an LLM end-to-end. They can write code, launch training, evaluate checkpoints, and improve downstream performance, raising the prospect of AI-for-AI. We argue that this picture conflates two distinct capabilities: execution-level capability, iterating within a selected training strategy; and strategy-level capability, revising the high-level judgment as experimental evidence accumulates. Analyzing a large corpus of publicly released post-training trajectories, we find that across different tasks, the agent's training strategy is locked in at the very beginning, and the entire remaining budget is spent on local adjustments within the selected strategy. We then examine three natural explanations--missing experience, missing guidance, and insufficient reasoning--with escalating interventions. Extensive experiments show that (1) an experience-driven scaffold improves execution across the board (+12.6 points on GSM8K and +40.8 on HumanEval) but leaves the strategy static; (2) human guidance effectively redirects the initial strategy, yet the agent falls back into local adjustment loops once training starts; and (3) additional inference compute pays off on easier tasks but yields almost no gain on the hardest one. In conclusion, what agents lack is neither experience, guidance, nor reasoning compute, but a mechanism for spontaneously reevaluating their strategy during execution.

item.title: Open-MOPD: Diagnosing and Fixing Capability Imbalance in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.19098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for consolidating domain-specialized reinforcement learning (RL) experts into a single generalist student via dense, token-level reward supervision. Despite its practical success, the optimization dynamics governing multi-teacher capability integration remain poorly understood, and open, rigorously reproducible recipes are conspicuously lacking. In this work, we establish a controlled M-OPD benchmark on SmolLM3-3B-Base with oracle routing, isolating capability integration from routing ambiguity. Our investigation reveals a pronounced capability integration gap: standard M-OPD captures only 35.6% of the available headroom relative to a domain-routed oracle ensemble, with concise tasks such as instruction following suffering severe degradation and premature stagnation. Crucially, we show that this failure stems not from gradient conflict, but from a severe misallocation of the token-level optimization budget. This pathology is driven by three orthogonal factors: structural sequence-length disparities across domains, dynamic convergence drift due to non-uniform learning rates, and multi-step reward staleness from asynchronous policy updates. To resolve these imbalances, we introduce Open-MOPD, a principled framework incorporating token-share balancing, gap-aware dynamic budget allocation, and student reward refresh. Together, these mechanisms systematically restore cross-domain balance, elevating headroom recovery from 35.6% to 83.4% in a single deployable student. We fully open-source our end-to-end post-training recipe, training trajectories, and evaluation suites on an academically accessible hardware budget.

item.title: Beyond Teacher Likelihood: Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.19181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using dense token-level guidance from a stronger teacher. In long-context tasks, however, token-level teacher support can favor locally plausible responses that omit evidence distributed across the input or violate global task constraints. Task-specific verifiers, in contrast, evaluate task completion at the response level and may return graded rewards that reflect partial success. We diagnose this mismatch on fixed responses from two representative long-context evidence-aggregation tasks. Across longer input ranges, trajectory-level OPD scores become progressively less aligned with verifier rewards, indicating teacher-verifier disagreement. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (GC-OPD). GC-OPD separately normalizes verifier rewards and trajectory-level OPD scores within each rollout group and uses their difference as a signed teacher-verifier disagreement residual. Relative-advantage-based credit assignment (RACA) distributes this trajectory-level residual across tokens according to their relative OPD advantages while preserving the original OPD signal. Across five long-context benchmarks, post-training with GC-OPD raises the five-benchmark averages of the official Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B checkpoints from 29.08 to 40.47 and from 35.12 to 44.65, respectively. Vanilla OPD reaches 39.31 and 43.56 under the same setup. Controlled ablations show that the signed residual is more effective than either an additional OPD-derived term or direct group-normalized verifier reward addition, while RACA further improves over uniform token allocation. Together, these results demonstrate that group-relative residual calibration can incorporate verifier outcomes without discarding dense token-level guidance. Code is available at https://github.com/SolereZhang/GC-OPD.

item.title: MedStruct-S: A Benchmark for Key Discovery, Key-Conditioned QA and Semi-Structured Extraction from OCR Clinical Reports [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.03103v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Semi-structured information extraction (IE) from OCR-derived clinical reports is crucial for efficiently reconstructing patients' longitudinal medical histories. In practice, this scenario commonly involves three tasks: (i) field-header (key) discovery, (ii) key-conditioned question answering (QA), and (iii) end-to-end key-value pair extraction. However, existing evaluations often under-model two factors: heterogeneous and incompletely known key representations, and OCR-induced noise. This makes it difficult to assess model robustness in real-world settings. We present MedStruct-S, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate these tasks under unknown keys and OCR noise. MedStruct-S contains 3,582 annotated real-world clinical report pages. Using MedStruct-S, we benchmark two representative paradigms: encoder-only sequence labeling with post-processing and decoder-only structured generation, covering four encoder-only and five decoder-only models spanning 0.11B to 103B parameters. Our results show that encoder-only models achieve the best performance for non-null-value key-conditioned QA despite being substantially smaller than decoder-only models. When comparing models of similar order of magnitude, encoder-only models still perform better overall. Without controlling for model scale, fine-tuned decoder-only models deliver the strongest overall results. These findings show that the benchmark provides a reliable and practical basis for selecting and comparing models across different semi-structured IE settings.

item.title: Jailbreaking in the Haystack [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2511.04707v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in long-context language models (LMs) have enabled million-token inputs, expanding their capabilities across complex tasks like computer-use agents. Yet, the safety implications of these extended contexts remain unclear. To bridge this gap, we introduce NINJA (short for Needle-in-haystack jailbreak attack), a method that jailbreaks aligned LMs by appending benign, model-generated content to harmful user goals. Critical to our method is the observation that the position of harmful goals play an important role in safety. Experiments on standard safety benchmark, HarmBench, show that NINJA significantly increases attack success rates across state-of-the-art open and proprietary models, including LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, and Gemini. Unlike prior jailbreaking methods, our approach is low-resource, transferable, and less detectable. Moreover, we show that NINJA is compute-optimal -- under a fixed compute budget, increasing context length can outperform increasing the number of trials in best-of-N jailbreak. These findings reveal that even benign long contexts -- when crafted with careful goal positioning -- introduce fundamental vulnerabilities in modern LMs.

item.title: SkillNet: Create, Evaluate, and Connect AI Skills [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.04448v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current AI agents can flexibly invoke tools and execute complex tasks, yet their long-term advancement is hindered by the lack of systematic accumulation and transfer of skills. Without a unified mechanism for skill consolidation, agents frequently ``reinvent the wheel'', rediscovering solutions in isolated contexts without leveraging prior strategies. To address this challenge, we introduce SkillNet, an open infrastructure for creating, evaluating, and organizing AI skills at scale. SkillNet structures skills within a unified ontology that supports creating skills from heterogeneous sources, establishing rich relational connections, and performing multi-dimensional evaluation across Safety, Completeness, Executability, Maintainability, and Cost-awareness. Our infrastructure integrates a repository of over 600,000 skills, an interactive platform, and a versatile Python toolkit. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show 40% higher average rewards and 30% fewer execution steps across multiple backbone models. Furthermore, SkillNet-Gym benchmarks skill retrieval, utilization, and composition, while SkillNet-Fabric enables task-specific skill routing through lightweight Wikis. By formalizing skills as evolving, composable assets, SkillNet provides a robust foundation for agents to move from transient experience to durable mastery.

item.title: Demystifying Training-Time Augmentation for Data-Constrained Language Model Pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.16246v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI labs approach a data ceiling where compute capacity outpaces the rate of new high-quality text generation, language model pretraining is shifting toward a data-constrained, compute-abundant regime that demands productive multi-epoch training on fixed corpora. Standard autoregressive (AR) pretraining overfits severely in this setting, reaching its optimum early and then continuously deteriorating. We investigate training-time data augmentation as a regularizer to mitigate this overfitting and enable productive training for hundreds of epochs on the same data. We introduce three orthogonal categories of augmentation for AR pretraining: token-level noise (masking, random replacement), sequence permutations (right-to-left prediction, Fill-in-the-Middle), and target offset prediction ($x_{t+i}$ for $i > 1$). Through systematic ablations, we find that individual augmentations delay overfitting and lower validation loss relative to the baseline, with random token replacement achieving the best minimum loss among individual methods. Combining augmentation categories further lowers the minimum validation loss. Our experiments demonstrate that data augmentations mitigate AR pretraining's data inefficiency and offer a promising solution to the data-constrained regime~\footnote{All code and data are available at https://github.com/ michaelchen-lab/ data-augmentations-for-pretraining.

item.title: Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.12036v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet the mechanisms underlying their capabilities and the risks they may pose remain poorly understood. As AI development becomes faster and increasingly automated, mechanistic exploration remains largely manual, widening the gap between what models can do and our ability to understand and control them. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mechanist, an agentic system that uses AI as a scientific instrument for the autonomous discovery of mechanisms underlying AI intelligence. To support autonomous mechanistic discovery, we construct an interpretability-focused knowledge graph of approximately 13,000 papers and integrate it with a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers spanning 26 fields. We further curate a library of 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation. Compared with Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems, Mechanist generates more valuable mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments more reliably. Mechanist also demonstrates a progression from discovering model behaviors to explaining and controlling AI models. Specifically, Mechanist first uncovers a counterintuitive safety risk in scientific laboratories, showing that unsafe traits can transfer across modalities through apparently safe training data. Mechanist then develops a mechanism theory of belief, revealing how models represent world knowledge, form beliefs, infer the beliefs of others, and how these mechanisms emerge during pretraining. Finally, Mechanist translates these mechanistic insights into practical interventions that improve model performance across diverse scenarios and steer scientific foundation models toward generating DNA sequences with specified properties.
